Good instinct to flag this. Based on how these proxies (jira-proxy.js, salesforce-proxy.js) are written, there are two concrete gaps     relative to what you're hoping is already true:      1. They're not actually localhost-only right now. They're started with http.createServer(...).listen(PORT, callback) — no host argument.        Node's default when you omit the host is to bind 0.0.0.0, i.e. all network interfaces, not just the loopback interface. So as        written, anything else on your LAN that can reach your machine's IP on that port could hit it — this isn't just a "hopefully"        situation, it's actually open beyond localhost today. The fix is to pass the host explicitly: .listen(PORT, '127.0.0.1', callback).     2. CORS is wide open: both set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, meaning any page loaded in the same browser — not just wigwag.html — can        make a cross-origin fetch to http://localhost:8934/:8936 and pull data through it, if it can guess the endpoint shape (which isn't        secret — it's public in this repo). That's a real vector even with correct localhost-only binding, since a malicious or compromised        tab running in your own browser is still "local" from the proxy's point of view.      Beyond fixing #1, a few things worth layering on:      - Tighten CORS to the actual origin wigwag is served from instead of * — trickier if you open wigwag.html via file:// (origin comes       through as null), but still narrows the surface for the common case of serving it over http.     - A shared-secret header: have wigwag's Settings hold a token that gets sent on every proxy request, and have the proxy reject anything       without it. This is the strongest single addition, because it defends against the "other local process/rogue tab" case that       localhost-only binding alone doesn't cover — binding restricts network origin, not same-machine origin.     - Minimize the exposure window: only run the proxy while you're actually linking things, then kill it, rather than leaving it up       indefinitely.     - One thing already done reasonably well: the startup/status logging only ever prints the auth mode (token / password-flow), never the       actual credentials or fetched record contents — so at least nothing sensitive is landing in a terminal scrollback or log file by       default.      The localhost-binding fix (#1) is the one I'd treat as not-optional — it's a real, currently-open gap, not a hypothetical one.

history.text:
Good instinct to flag this. Based on how these proxies (jira-proxy.js, salesforce-proxy.js) are written, there are two concrete gaps
    relative to what you're hoping is already true:

    1. They're not actually localhost-only right now. They're started with http.createServer(...).listen(PORT, callback) — no host argument.
       Node's default when you omit the host is to bind 0.0.0.0, i.e. all network interfaces, not just the loopback interface. So as
       written, anything else on your LAN that can reach your machine's IP on that port could hit it — this isn't just a "hopefully"
       situation, it's actually open beyond localhost today. The fix is to pass the host explicitly: .listen(PORT, '127.0.0.1', callback).
    2. CORS is wide open: both set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, meaning any page loaded in the same browser — not just wigwag.html — can
       make a cross-origin fetch to http://localhost:8934/:8936 and pull data through it, if it can guess the endpoint shape (which isn't
       secret — it's public in this repo). That's a real vector even with correct localhost-only binding, since a malicious or compromised
       tab running in your own browser is still "local" from the proxy's point of view.

    Beyond fixing #1, a few things worth layering on:

    - Tighten CORS to the actual origin wigwag is served from instead of * — trickier if you open wigwag.html via file:// (origin comes
      through as null), but still narrows the surface for the common case of serving it over http.
    - A shared-secret header: have wigwag's Settings hold a token that gets sent on every proxy request, and have the proxy reject anything
      without it. This is the strongest single addition, because it defends against the "other local process/rogue tab" case that
      localhost-only binding alone doesn't cover — binding restricts network origin, not same-machine origin.
    - Minimize the exposure window: only run the proxy while you're actually linking things, then kill it, rather than leaving it up
      indefinitely.
    - One thing already done reasonably well: the startup/status logging only ever prints the auth mode (token / password-flow), never the
      actual credentials or fetched record contents — so at least nothing sensitive is landing in a terminal scrollback or log file by
      default.

    The localhost-binding fix (#1) is the one I'd treat as not-optional — it's a real, currently-open gap, not a hypothetical one.

history.text: Fixed in b2179db. Root cause: renderVals() recomputed the sort live on every render, so editing a field in the currently-sorted column (e.g. Status/RAG) moved the row the instant the edit committed -- it visibly vanished from under the cursor mid-click. Now the row order is snapshotted right before a same-column edit commits and held for a short grace period, so the edit's new value shows in place first; the table settles into the real sorted order once the grace period elapses. An explicit re-sort/clear/project-switch drops the freeze immediately. New regression coverage in tests/interaction.spec.js.

Follow-up: found a gap in this fix while testing the new "clear a select field" feature -- sortSnapshot (the frozen order) was only ever computed by an explicit sortBy()/switchProject() call, never at initial page load. A fresh load with an already-persisted sort preference (the common case: sorted in an earlier session, then just reopened the tab) fell through to the live/unfrozen sort branch until the next explicit re-sort, reproducing the original jarring reorder on the very first edit. Fixed: sortSnapshot is now also computed once at boot, right after the initial project's issues load.

history.value: Connect Remote: no-access screen with per-identity failure reasons, re-authorize, request access

Right now a repo nothing can read just leaves the Connect button disabled in Connect Remote's probe sheet -- no explanation why, no next step. The remotes.zip design handoff's own 13c frame specifies a richer screen: per-identity failure reasons surfaced individually (expired token vs. never had access vs. repo doesn't exist -- probeGithubRepoAccess already returns a reason field for this, just unused downstream), a Re-authorize action for an expired token, a Request access action (needs its own design pass, nothing in this codebase sends outbound requests to a repo owner today), and reusing a credential that's already proven itself against a different remote (not designed in the source material either).
First write on a read-only-connected project

A project connected as public-read-only (or via a single identity that can read but not write) has no path today from having it open to actually changing something. The remotes.zip handoff frames this as an evolution of the existing first-write attribution gate (requireAttribution) rather than a new mechanism: the first edit on a read-only project should prompt for which identity is making the change, same as a null-identity Shared-with-you project's first write already does, but then needs an actual write path -- a fork, a PR, a queued-change-for-someone-with-push model -- that doesn't exist yet. Worth scoping once the underlying write-elsewhere mechanism is picked.
remotes[] plural data model for genuine fork/mirror support

A project's connection info is currently singular (githubRepo/githubRepoPath/githubRepoBranch on the doc, one identityId on the project record). Genuine fork/mirror support -- the same project reachable at two different addresses, or a local copy tracking an upstream it diverged from -- needs a plural remotes[] shape instead, with the existing two-copies-are-the-same-project-when-their-UUIDs-match-not-when-their-addresses-do dedup rule extended to say which remote is home. connectRemoteFinish's existing UUID-match-merges-in behaviour (see tests/connect-remote.spec.js) is the right foundation for this, not a replacement.

A hidden/backgrounded tab could silently starve GitHub sync polling forever

history.text: Reported live: footer said synced Nm ago while the actual GitHub file had a newer commit. Root cause: publishGithubLeaderStatus() kept heartbeating leadership even while its own tab was backgrounded, so a stale/forgotten hidden tab could hold the sync-leader claim indefinitely -- only the leader polls, and a hidden leader's own poll always no-ops by design, so remote changes stopped being picked up at all, silently. Fixed in 9b75f32: heartbeat publishing now also skips while hidden (so a hidden leader's claim goes stale), and a follower's own poll tick now claims leadership if the current holder has gone stale. New regression coverage in tests/github-sync.spec.js.

Follow-up polish: the pinned "— No value —" row was making the popover need an internal scroll for fields with enough options to nearly fill it (it was inside the scrollable list). Moved it to its own pinned row above the scrollable list, so it no longer counts against that budget.

history.value: Replace GitHub-sync leader election with visibility gating + ETag conditional polling

history.text: Deletes the localStorage-based leader-election scheme entirely (99d805a) and replaces it with document.hidden as the sole gate on connect/poll/push -- every visible tab now syncs independently, no shared claim to go stale (this structurally supersedes the fix in #43, which patched the leader-election system rather than removing it). A visibilitychange-triggered onBecameVisible makes a hidden-then-refocused tab catch up immediately instead of waiting for the next interval. Follow-up commit (57dd539) adds ETag/If-None-Match conditional polling so a routine no-op poll doesn't count against GitHub's rate limit at all, offsetting the accepted tradeoff of multiple visible tabs each polling independently. Full plan at the time: /home/dev/.claude/plans/vast-cuddling-pnueli.md (local to the session that did this work). One thing worth a live check: the ETag approach depends on GitHub's real Contents API sending Access-Control-Expose-Headers for the ETag header cross-origin -- confirmed necessary and mocked correctly in tests, but unverifiable against the real API from that sandboxed session (no internet access). If it's not exposed in practice, polling just silently reverts to the pre-ETag behavior -- not broken, just no extra savings.

history.value: Cross-project data leak: startMerge is now guarded against a mismatched or stale projectId

history.text:
Root-caused and fixed. startMerge() is the single real merge function every caller goes through, but the GitHub sync path (connectGithubRepo, pollGithubForRemoteChanges) never checked whether a fetched file's own declared projectId matched the project it was being merged into -- and both are async functions that never re-checked state.projectId after their awaits either. Switching projects while a connect/poll was still in flight could apply a stale result (the merge itself, sha/etag bookkeeping, sync status) to whatever project happened to be active by the time it resolved.

Confirmed via a git-stash A/B that this reproduces the real reported bug exactly: reverting just the fix leaks a synced project's full issue list into a brand-new blank project when the connect resolves mid-switch.

Two independent layers now in place: (1) startMerge() itself refuses to merge content whose own declared projectId doesn't match the active project (the one legitimate caller that deliberately merges a foreign-declared file after an explicit user confirm -- Apply update's mismatch dialog -- opts out via a new allowProjectMismatch flag); (2) connectGithubRepo/pollGithubForRemoteChanges/pushToGithub each capture their project id up front and re-check it after every await.

Landed as commit 42e1019, with two new regression tests in tests/github-sync.spec.js. Full suite passes (500/500, only the two pre-existing KNOWN GAP staleness tests show their usual soft-fail marker). Related to #43/#45 (same GitHub-sync area, same session).

history.value: wigwag-core Phase 3: design a Store interface for the signed-write path

history.text: The real design problem Phases 1/2 don't touch: appendSignedHistory/appendProjectHistory do an optimistic setState (unsigned entry), sign async, then a second setState patching the signature on -- inherently React-setState-shaped. Plan: split each mutation into a pure compute function (e.g. computeSelectOption -> {changed, historyEntryDraft}) plus one shared commitHistoryEntry(store, ...) owning the two-phase write generically against a small Store interface (getIssue/appendEntry/patchEntrySignature/nextSortKey) -- wigwag.html implements Store via setState, a CLI implements it with in-memory state + a file write. Highest value, highest risk -- needs its own dedicated planning pass before implementation.

The two-phase optimistic-then-signed commit pattern turned out to be duplicated 6 times (not 2 as originally scoped): appendSignedHistory, appendProjectHistory, addComment, saveEditComment, postProjectComment, saveEditProjectComment. Moved the shared orchestration into wigwag-core.js as commitSignedEntry(entryBase, payloads, store), plus importSigningKey/signWithKey/verifyPayload and advanceSortKey (the sortKey counter arithmetic). The six methods in wigwag.html now build entry/payloads as before and delegate the actual commit to a small store closure -- external call sites of those six methods are unchanged. history.value: Make wigwag into a full LLM interaction model

I like the direction, but "notifications on change" is necessary and not sufficient — a few other pieces need to exist before conversations can actually live in tickets rather than just being logged there:

Notifications themselves — wigwag has no push/poll-to-user channel today; the GitHub sync layer polls GitHub, but nothing watches the local tracker and tells a human "something changed." You'd need either a lightweight watcher (desktop notification, email, Slack webhook) triggered off the signed-history append, or a digest/mention model so people aren't pinged on every field edit — just comments and @-mentions aimed at them.

@-mentions and a notion of "who's this comment for." Comments today are just history entries — nobody is addressed. Real conversation needs a way to say "this needs Thomas" vs "just a log entry," or every comment becomes a notification to everyone watching the issue.

Read/unread state per user. Otherwise every reopen of an issue looks unchanged-vs-new the same way, and conversation threads become unnavigable once they're more than a couple comments deep.

Faster round-trip than the current GitHub-sync path. Right now writes go through a push-debounce and conditional-polling pull cycle — fine for backlog grooming, way too laggy for back-and-forth conversation. Real-time-feeling chat needs either a much shorter poll interval or a proper push channel (websocket/SSE) rather than the current ETag-polling model.

Threading/reply structure, since comments are currently a flat append-only log — fine for a decision trail, less fine for "which of these three points are you responding to" once a conversation gets going.

I'd treat notifications as the trigger that makes this worth doing at all, but mentions + read state are what actually make it usable as a conversation medium rather than a fancy activity log.

history.text:
Design sketch: instead of a live chat session driving Claude Code work, wigwag issues become the sole decision channel -- Tom files/comments on issues, Claude periodically checks the tracker and acts.

Scoping (for now): an issue with Status = "Next" is in Claude's scope to pick up and act on. Nothing else -- Todo/In Progress/Blocked/Done/Won't Do issues are never touched autonomously, only ones Tom has explicitly promoted to Next. In the fullness of time this probably wants a real Assignee field instead (so scoping isn't overloaded onto the same field that also tracks workflow state), but Status=Next is sufficient to start.

Loop mechanism: Claude Code's own ScheduleWakeup dynamic-loop primitive, checking on a slow cadence (20-30 min, matching wigwag-agent.js's own ~10-20s-per-call cost against a real shared tracker with other concurrent editors) -- not a tight loop.

Per-issue flow once picked up: Claude moves Status to "In Progress" (visible signal it's being worked, and removes it from the next poll's Next-scan), does the work, comments on the issue with what it did (same pattern as the mention-notification comment on #70 this session), then moves Status to "Done" -- or "Blocked" with a comment explaining what it's blocked on, if it can't proceed without Tom's input. Tom's replies/comments on a Blocked or even Done issue while Claude is between polls are how follow-up direction gets back in, without ever needing a live chat session.

Needed pieces:
- A polling script (list issues where Status==Next, scoped to this project) -- built as part of this issue, using wigwag-client.js's list() which already resolves Status labels.
- The ScheduleWakeup loop wiring to actually run this on a cadence.
- Judgment calls each iteration still needs a real Claude Code turn (reading the issue, deciding how to act) -- the polling script only answers "is there work," it doesn't do the work itself.

Safety: this is a live, shared tracker other real users edit (per this repo's own CLAUDE.md) -- scope is deliberately narrow (Status=Next only, never proactively touching other issues/other users' items) to keep blast radius small while this is being trialled.

Live-validated: you set #66 to Next, the loop's next scheduled poll hadn't fired yet (~25min cadence), so I picked it up directly when you asked live rather than waiting -- confirms the Next-status scoping and the In Progress -> comment -> Done workflow both work end to end (see #66's own comments). The ScheduleWakeup loop is running in the background on its normal cadence going forward; direction from here comes via marking issues Next or commenting on Blocked/Done ones, as designed. history.value: ARCHITECTURE ISSUE: How should we consider identity across instances?

My email is tom@lant.uk for this identity. Each session is currently signed with a different key. I don't think that the email and the key are actually entangled. But it will be common for folks to work across multiple instances. How should this be managed? The key really just guards against silliness. Can you come back on this issue with some thoughts?

history.text:
You're right that email and key aren't entangled -- that's by design, and it's already written down in docs/FORMAT.md's 'Identity and signing' section: 'This is explicitly not a security boundary. The email is self-proclaimed, not verified by any authority... a lightweight who-did-this-and-was-it-tampered-with mechanism for collaborators who are basically trusting each other already.' The signature's real job is tamper-evidence (did this entry's content change after it was signed), not authentication (is this really that person).

Interesting finding: the docs (and a code comment in wigwag-core.js) already describe an intended answer to your exact question -- a TOFU (trust-on-first-use) identity store that remembers which pubkey an email used first, and flags a LATER import claiming the same email with a DIFFERENT key as 'a possible impersonation attempt'. But I checked, and it's not actually wired up anywhere -- verifyPayload() is imported into wigwag.html's Component class but never once called. So today, literally nothing checks key-per-email consistency at all; the docs describe a plan that was never implemented.

Given that gap, I'd actually caution against implementing TOFU exactly as documented, because of the exact scenario you raised: since multi-device use is common, and each device/browser generates its own key independently the first time it's opened, strict TOFU would false-positive constantly -- your own laptop and phone, both legitimately you, would look like 'impersonation' to each other the moment their data merges, since each device's local TOFU store only ever saw ITS OWN key as tom@lant.uk's 'first' one.

My recommendation: don't try to pin one key per email at all. Keep email as the human-facing attribution/grouping label (already true everywhere), and let pubKey mean 'which device/session produced this', full stop -- multiple legitimate keys per email is the normal case, not an anomaly to flag. If you want SOME visibility here later, I'd suggest something soft and informational rather than a security alarm -- e.g. a project could note 'tom@lant.uk has signed from 3 different keys' as a fact, not a warning -- but I wouldn't build even that without a concrete reason it'd help, given the doc's own explicit stance that this was never meant to resist a motivated adversary. Filed the soft/informational version as a separate backlog item (not Next) in case you want to revisit it later -- this issue's core question feels answered as 'no action needed, current behavior is fine and matches the documented intent once you drop the never-implemented TOFU-alarm idea'.

history.value: We will need a way for multiple tabs signed in with the same email/identity/session to avoid sending mulitple push notifications, unless this is already handled at another layer of deduping?

history.text:
Fixed: the Notification API's own `tag` option now dedupes this at the browser level -- new Notification(title, { body, tag: 'wigwag-mention-' + commentId }) in checkForNewMentions. Two independent fire attempts for the same comment (from two tabs racing, or a same-tab retry) share the same tag, so the OS replaces rather than stacks them -- only one visible notification ever, regardless of timing.

This is a different, narrower layer than NOTIFIED_MENTIONS_KEY (the existing localStorage-based 'have we told the user about this' set): that already prevents re-notifying about the same comment on a LATER poll, but it's a check-then-act read+write with no cross-tab locking, so two tabs polling independently (no leader election, by design) could both decide 'not yet notified' in the same race window before either writes back. The tag fix closes exactly that gap natively, without needing any actual cross-tab coordination/locking.

Covered by a new test in tests/mentions.spec.js asserting the tag is derived from the comment's own id, plus a direct simulation of a second near-simultaneous fire collapsing into the same notification. Full suite: 606/606 passing.

history.value: What's the quickest way to get a version of this running on my phone that works with push notifications and syncs through to the github backend?

history.text:
Investigated the current code (no PWA infra exists yet -- confirmed via search: no manifest.json, no service worker, no Push API/pushManager use anywhere in wigwag.html; notifications today are plain `new Notification()` calls that only fire while a tab is literally open, per the mention-notification work earlier this session). Two real paths, and they don't have the same "quickest" answer for the app-shell vs. the push part:

**Getting the app itself on your phone -- quick, ~PWA:**
Mobile-responsive UI (row list/detail, header, switcher sheets) already shipped in Phase 1, and GitHub sync already runs client-side against the existing OAuth proxy the same way on mobile as desktop -- no new backend needed for sync. The fast path is turning wigwag.html into an installable PWA: add a `manifest.json` + app icons + a minimal service worker (even just for offline-cache/installability, no push logic required yet), then "Add to Home Screen" on the phone. This needs no native toolchain at all, which matters because **this devcontainer has neither Android SDK nor Xcode** -- only the Linux desktop Rust/webkit2gtk toolchain for the existing Tauri build. That's genuinely a day-ish of work, not a big lift.

**Push notifications when the app isn't open -- the actually hard part, same difficulty either way:**
Today's notification mechanism requires an open, polling tab -- there's no server that knows when new tracker content lands except whichever client happens to be open. Real "notify me even when the app is closed" needs: a service worker + Web Push subscription (VAPID keys) + a server-side relay that watches the repo (e.g. a GitHub webhook receiver, similar in shape to `jira-proxy.js`/`salesforce-proxy.js`) and fans out push messages to subscribed devices. That's genuinely new backend infrastructure, not a wrapper choice -- and it's needed **regardless** of whether you go PWA or native.

One more real constraint: if your phone is an iPhone, Web Push only works for a PWA actually installed to the home screen (iOS 16.4+) -- it does not work in a plain Safari tab. Worth confirming which platform this is for.

**Tauri Mobile** (Tauri 2, which we already use, does support `ios init`/`android init`) would give true native push via platform channels, but doesn't remove the webhook-relay problem above, and adds real setup cost this environment doesn't have today: Xcode/Android Studio toolchains (a Dockerfile change + rebuild, and this container still couldn't run an iOS build without a macOS host), code signing, and an Apple Developer Program membership for anything beyond a 7-day free-provisioning install. For "quickest," it's a strictly bigger lift than PWA for the same amount of push-infra work.

**Recommendation:** start with the PWA path to get something installed on your phone fast, and treat "real push when closed" as a separate follow-up needing a small webhook-relay server -- worth its own issue once scoped, since it's new infrastructure rather than a UI tweak. Marking this Blocked pending your call on: (a) PWA vs. native as the wrapper, and (b) whether to scope the webhook-relay push work now or later, and which platform (iOS/Android) to prioritize.
This would be for iOS, so if an installed PWA can receive web push and push changes of its own to github then happy days

Shipped the PWA + push side for iOS, per your call to go the installed-PWA + self-hosted-relay route. Summary:

**Installability** (automatic, nothing to configure): `manifest.json` + a minimal `sw.js` now ship alongside `wigwag.html`, with the real rendered head (not the outer loading-screen shell -- see docs/EDITING.md's two-layer structure) gaining a manifest link, apple-touch-icon, and the apple-mobile-web-app-* meta tags iOS actually reads (it mostly ignores the Manifest spec's own icon/display hints). Open the tracker over http(s)-- not a local file:// copy, service workers can't register there -- and use Share > Add to Home Screen.

**Push delivery while closed**: new `push-relay.js` (root) is a small self-hosted process -- `npm run push-relay` -- that polls the SAME tracker.jsonl your project already syncs with (reusing wigwag-core.js's own pullGithubFile/parseJsonl/textMentionsEmail, not a reimplementation) and sends a real Web Push message via VAPID whenever a new comment mentions a subscribed email. It only needs outbound internet -- no public address, no webhook setup, matching how the app's own background sync already works. Settings > Notifications > "Push notifications (beta)" has the relay URL/secret fields and an "Enable push notifications on this device" button, which refuses to proceed outside an installed (standalone) context with a clear message, exactly like iOS itself requires.

Verification: 8 new Playwright tests (tests/push-notifications.spec.js) cover the installability tags, settings UI, the full subscribe flow (stubbed service worker/pushManager, since a real subscribe would need actual network access to Apple/Google's push services), and error paths. push-relay.js itself was smoke-tested by hand against the real lampholder/wigwag repo (real GitHub poll, real mention detection found the real backlog of mentions in this tracker, real webpush.sendNotification calls -- only failing on the deliberately-fake test subscription key, as expected). Full suite: 613 passed, 2 pre-existing known-gap tests (unrelated, deliberately marked), 1 flaky cross-tab test confirmed passing in isolation.

One real bug caught and fixed along the way: my first draft of sw.js had a blanket passthrough `fetch` event handler ("just in case a platform's installability check wants one") -- once a service worker controls a page, that handler intercepts EVERY request the page makes, including the app's own GitHub/Jira/Salesforce calls, bypassing Playwright's request mocking entirely. Caught by a full-suite run (20 unrelated tests failed), root-caused, and removed -- there's no caching need to justify having one at all right now.

What I couldn't verify from here (needs your actual iPhone): real Add to Home Screen install, real permission prompt, and an actual push arriving while the app is fully closed. If anything's off on-device, comment here or file a follow-up and I'll pick it up. Marking Done since the implementation, tests, and manual smoke-testing are all clean -- flag it back to Next if real-device testing turns up something.

history.value: PWA: detect and prompt for updates instead of silently serving a stale resumed instance

history.text:
Context: Tom asked in chat whether there's a nice way for PWAs to get updated -- this is that discussion, filed as a proper issue per his standing instruction to always file ideas/suggestions this way rather than leaving them in chat.

The problem isn't wigwag's service worker (sw.js) itself -- it's deliberately minimal, existing only to satisfy Web Push's requirement for a registered SW (self.skipWaiting() + clients.claim(), no fetch handler, no asset caching at all -- see sw.js's own header comment, added for #72). So there's no stale service-worker cache to bust.

The real cause is a well-known installed-PWA quirk on iOS/Android: tapping the home-screen icon often resumes the existing in-memory page instance instead of doing a fresh network load, so code changes sitting on the server never reach the app until something forces a real reload.

Recommended fix: a lightweight version check on the page's visibilitychange event. When the app comes back to the foreground, fetch a tiny version marker file with cache:'no-store'; if it differs from what's currently loaded, show a small non-intrusive 'Update available -- tap to reload' banner rather than reloading silently. Deliberately NOT a silent auto-reload -- wigwag has real local in-progress drafts (comment drafts, edit-in-progress cells, etc.) that a surprise reload would blow away, so surfacing it as a dismissible prompt the user acts on is the safer choice.

Sketch:
- A small static file (e.g. version.txt or version.json) containing a build identifier, updated whenever wigwag.html changes (could be a content hash, a timestamp, or a manually bumped version string).
- A visibilitychange listener (only when document.visibilityState becomes 'visible') that fetches that file with {cache: 'no-store'}, compares it against a copy embedded in the page at load time, and if different, sets a small piece of UI state to show the banner.
- Banner action just does location.reload() (a real network navigation, which will pick up the fresh wigwag.html).
- Should also fire once on initial load in case the version already drifted while the tab was closed, not just on later visibility changes.

Not started -- filed for triage/prioritization, not picked up as work yet.

Picking this up. One change from my earlier sketch above: rather than a separately-maintained version.txt/version.json that has to be manually bumped on every deploy (easy to forget, and this project deliberately has no build step to automate that), I'll compare HTTP Last-Modified instead -- a plain HEAD request (cache: 'no-store') against the currently-loaded page's own document.lastModified. Static file hosts (GitHub Pages, S3, nginx, etc.) already send an accurate Last-Modified for a plain file with zero extra deploy steps, so this can't drift out of sync with a real deploy the way a manually-bumped marker could.

Plan:
- New checkForAppUpdate() method: skip entirely on file: origins or inside the Tauri desktop app (neither has this staleness problem -- Tauri updates via its own installer). Otherwise HEAD-fetch the current path with cache:'no-store', read the Last-Modified response header, and compare its timestamp against document.lastModified (the value the currently-running page itself was served with). A network failure or a host that omits the header just skips quietly that cycle -- fails open, tries again next time.
- Called once from componentDidMount (covers 'the version already drifted while this tab/PWA instance was closed') and again from the existing visibilitychange handler (covers 'came back to the foreground after a while').
- New appUpdateAvailable state flag drives a small dismissible banner (styled like the existing deep-link-notice toast), bottom-right, with a 'Reload' action (location.reload()) and a ✕ to dismiss without reloading -- never a silent auto-reload, since in-progress drafts (comment text, edit-in-progress cells) would get blown away.
- Durable tests: mock the HEAD response's Last-Modified via page.route, verify the banner appears only when the server's timestamp is newer, verify Reload/dismiss actions, verify it's skipped on file: origin.

Done. Implemented as a plain HTTP freshness check rather than the version.txt sketch above -- no build step in this project to keep a manually-bumped marker in sync, but a static file host's own Last-Modified header can't drift out of sync with a real deploy.

checkForAppUpdate(): a HEAD request (cache:'no-store') to the page's own path, comparing the response's Last-Modified against document.lastModified (what this running instance was actually served with). Runs once on mount (catches drift while the tab/PWA instance was closed) and again on every visibilitychange (catches a deploy landing while it sat backgrounded). Skips entirely on file: origins and inside the Tauri desktop app -- neither has this staleness problem. A small dismissible bottom-right banner ('Update available' / Reload / ✕) drives the actual reload -- never silent, so an in-progress draft (comment text, edit-in-progress cell) survives a dismiss.

8 new tests in tests/app-update-notice.spec.js: banner on newer Last-Modified, none on older, missing-header and network-failure cases fail silently with no crash, Reload does a real navigation, dismiss preserves an in-progress edit, re-checks on visibilitychange not just mount, skipped inside a Tauri stub. Full suite (706 tests) passed clean.

history.value: measureTableOverflow() can enter a genuine infinite re-render loop (React 'Maximum update depth exceeded'), pinning a CPU core

history.text:
Root cause (found while investigating an unrelated issue earlier, not yet fixed): measureTableOverflow() computes `overflows = (el.scrollHeight - currentSpacer) > (el.clientHeight + 1)`, where currentSpacer depends on the PREVIOUS render's own tableOverflow state -- a self-referential height measurement. In a narrow band near the threshold, this can genuinely oscillate: setting tableOverflow triggers a re-render, which changes currentSpacer, which flips the measurement back, which triggers another re-render, forever. Confirmed via a live repro at the time: a real React 'Maximum update depth exceeded' (error #185) loop, using a small imported project plus a couple of edits -- did NOT reproduce with the standard demo fixture's usual row count, so it's specifically tied to certain table-content heights landing in that narrow oscillation band.

Tom confirmed today (2026-09-07) he genuinely triggered this live, and it manifested as real fan/CPU load (though at the moment he checked Firefox's about:performance just now, no wigwag tab was actively spinning -- consistent with the loop only running while that specific narrow-band table height condition holds, not continuously).

Not fixed yet -- flagged instead of patched blind under time pressure, since measureTableOverflow's height-measurement logic is central to the table-overflow-indicator feature and touching it risks a real regression across the existing table-overflow test coverage. Needs someone to actually sit down with a reliable repro (a small imported project + a couple of edits, not the demo fixture) and redesign the measurement to not be self-referential -- e.g. comparing against the actual DOM's current scrollHeight/clientHeight directly each render rather than a value derived from the previous render's own state.

Unrelated fix landed alongside this while investigating #131: measureTableOverflow() is now gated so it runs far less often overall (only when row-layout-affecting state actually changes, not on every render). This reduces how often the self-referential tableOverflow measurement in this bug's own description gets evaluated at all, which may make the oscillation rarer in practice -- but the actual self-referential math (currentSpacer derived from the previous render's own tableOverflow state) is untouched. Still needs its own dedicated repro session per this issue's own prior note, not fixed here.

history.value: closeSlideOver() could silently discard a pending field edit (no blur = no commit)

history.text:
Found while investigating Tom's live report of a description-field edit not persisting (2026-09-08) -- the specific 'only works after opening DevTools' symptom itself was not reproduced (Tom confirmed he couldn't trigger it again), but this real, confirmed gap turned up along the way and is worth fixing regardless.

Root cause: closeSlideOver() tore down slide-over state (slideOverVisible, newCommentDraft, etc.) but never checked for or committed a pending activeCell edit first. Every text field (including the description field, which reuses the same buildCell/activeCell/editDraft machinery as a regular table cell) commits on blur, not via an explicit Save button -- so this was invisible for the common case of a real mouse click on the scrim or the X button, since that naturally blurs the focused input first (standard DOM event ordering: mousedown on the scrim moves focus away, firing blur, before the click handler that calls closeSlideOver even runs).

The gap only shows up on a PROGRAMMATIC close with no real blur involved at all -- e.g. the mobile bottom sheet's swipe-to-dismiss gesture (a touch drag, not a click), which also calls closeSlideOver(). Confirmed concretely: start editing a field inline (e.g. a date field via M7's own picker, which shares the same commit path), swipe the sheet away without ever blurring the input, and the edit was silently lost.

Fix: closeSlideOver() now checks if activeCell belongs to the currently-open issue and calls commitEdit() on it before proceeding, matching the existing 'blur commits' convention every text field already has (distinct from notes/comments, which use an explicit save button and intentionally discard on close -- this only affects the activeCell-based inline-edit path).

Covered by a new test: edit a mobile date field inline, swipe-dismiss the sheet mid-edit (no blur), reopen, confirm the value committed. Full suite: 649 passed, only the one already-known-flaky pre-existing test (interaction.spec.js:797) failed, reconfirmed flaky via 3 isolated reruns immediately after.

Plan for header.zip ("Per-Project Generated Header Background"): a unique, deterministic low-poly triangulated mesh background behind the header bar, seeded from the project's own UUID, with a scrim + fixed-ink text so it stays legible regardless of the generated palette.

Two deliberate deviations from the reference handoff, both because it's a design mockup and wigwag is the real app:

1. No Trianglify/CDN dependency. Wigwag is a single-file, no-build-step, offline-capable app (Tauri desktop + PWA) with zero runtime CDN scripts anywhere today. Same idea as Trianglify, no external script, works offline.

2. The header scrim uses a fixed light color, not var(--surface). The reference is light-mode-only; wigwag has a real dark theme where --surface is a *dark* oklch value. The whole point of the scrim is guaranteeing the fixed-dark-ink breadcrumb/caret text stays legible against an arbitrary mesh palette -- a dark scrim in dark mode would defeat that. The header action buttons' own translucent chips stay theme-driven (var(--surface) via color-mix), matching the reference exactly, since their text is theme-driven too and stays in sync.

Will verify with a CSS-var audit (no new undefined custom properties -- using fixed hex colors for the ink/scrim, not new theme vars) and the full suite before closing out.

history.value: All rendered links should always open in a new tab

history.text:
Investigated before touching anything: every hardcoded link in wigwag.html (GitHub/Jira/Salesforce/wigwag ref links, markdown-autolinked URLs in comments/notes/text fields) already carries target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" -- the only two exceptions are the wigwag: cross-project reference pills, which are deliberately in-app navigation (href="#", intercepted by a click handler), not real external links; that's existing, tested behavior and out of scope here.

So in a plain browser this already works. The real gap is the Tauri desktop app: its src-tauri/Cargo.toml has no shell/opener plugin configured at all, and its capabilities file only grants "core:default". Tauri's webview doesn't automatically route target="_blank" clicks to the system's default browser without one -- depending on the platform's webview engine, it likely either does nothing or tries to open the link inside the app's own window, which isn't a real "new tab" at all. That's almost certainly what you're seeing.

Plan: add tauri-plugin-opener (the standard Tauri v2 plugin for this), register it in main.rs, grant its permission in capabilities/default.json, enable withGlobalTauri so wigwag.html can call it without an ESM bundler, and add a small click-intercept in wigwag.html: when running inside Tauri (window.__TAURI__ present), route target="_blank" anchor clicks through the plugin's openUrl instead of the webview's native handling; in a plain browser/PWA, target="_blank" already works natively and is left untouched.

This needs a Tauri rebuild to take effect (Rust changes), which I can attempt via cargo in this sandbox to verify it compiles, but the actual desktop app needs rebuilding on your end to pick it up -- I'll flag that clearly once the code changes are in and verified to build.

Added tauri-plugin-opener (Cargo.toml + main.rs registration + "opener:default" capability), enabled withGlobalTauri, and a frontend click-intercept that calls the plugin's open_url command for target=_blank clicks -- but only when window.__TAURI__ is actually present, so plain browser/PWA behavior is completely untouched. cargo check passes clean. 4 new tests in tests/tauri-external-links.spec.js. history.value: Implement date filtering by implementing date_filter.zip

history.text:
Plan: date-type columns get the same "..." menu FILTER section select/multiselect columns already have (same header, same Clear link, same isFiltered funnel-icon indicator), but with a date-range control instead of a checkbox list -- matching the handoff's own design. Presets (Today / Last 7 days / Last 30 days / This month) as quick-pick rows, highlighted when active, plus two native date inputs for a custom range. A row matches when its value is >= from (if set) AND <= to (if set); a row with no value never matches an active filter (excluded, not a wildcard) -- both exactly as specified.

The existing columnFilters map already supports this without a new storage key: it just needs a second value shape (`{from, to}` for date columns, vs the array-of-option-ids shape for select/multiselect) -- issueValueMatchesFilter and computeColumnFilterExcludedIds (both in wigwag-core.js, shared with wigwag.html's hand-synced embedded copy) get a new date-type branch, and the "is this filter active" check needs to handle both shapes (array length vs from/to presence) since it currently only checks .length.

One departure from literal porting: "today" needs computing in the LOCAL calendar day, not UTC (new Date().toISOString() shifts across midnight depending on timezone offset) -- writing a small local-date helper and a pure, testable dateFilterPresetRanges(now) function (takes "now" as a parameter so it's testable with a fixed date) rather than hardcoding Date.now() calls inline.

Done. Implemented the full date_filter.zip design: column "..." menu now shows a FILTER section for date-type fields with Today / Last 7 days / Last 30 days / This month presets (active preset bolded + tinted) plus a custom From/To range via two native date inputs. Matching semantics: inclusive ISO string comparison on both bounds, a row with no value for the field never matches an active filter, and clearing both bounds removes the filter entirely -- reuses the existing columnFilters map with a new {from,to} shape for date columns (array-of-ids stays the shape for select/multiselect). Local calendar-day computation (getFullYear/getMonth/getDate) used throughout instead of toISOString() to avoid UTC off-by-one-day bugs.

Found and fixed two real bugs along the way:
1. A genuine crash: the pre-existing filterOptions array-builder ran unconditionally for every column and called .includes() on activeColumnFilter -- for a date column that's now an object {from,to}, not an array, so opening a date column's menu crashed the whole render. Guarded it to skip building that array for date-type columns.
2. A genuine layout/positioning bug: I first laid the From/To inputs out side-by-side, which made the menu wider than the fixed 200px the anchor-clamping logic assumes when keeping menus on-screen -- so for a date column at/near the right edge of the table, the menu (and its Clear link) rendered off the right edge of the viewport, unreachable. Fixed by stacking From/To vertically (label + input per row), which keeps the menu at its normal ~200px width. Worth flagging generally: any popup content added to that shared column-menu needs to stay within its assumed clamp width, or the anchor math needs to learn the real rendered width.

history.value: Does it make sense for the View Source tab to show the size of the project file in megabytes?

history.text:
Looked into this. The View Source tab (data-testid=source-view) currently shows just the filename in its header and the pretty-printed jsonl body -- no size indicator of any kind. The raw text is already available cheaply via buildSourceText('full').length (this is exactly what's used to build the exported file and the pretty-printed view), so adding a size figure next to the filename is a small, low-risk change.

Where I think it's genuinely useful, not just decorative: the source file is an append-only log -- history entries accumulate forever and there's no auto-compaction (only an explicit 'squashed' export mode a user has to choose). That means project size grows monotonically over the life of a tracker, and GitHub itself cares about this: it soft-warns in the UI above 50MB and hard-rejects a single file over 100MB via both the API and git. A visible size figure gives an early, ambient signal of a project trending toward that territory long before it becomes a problem -- more useful than 'is this thing getting big' being invisible until a push mysteriously fails.

One thing I'd push back on: literally always showing megabytes. Two possibilities I can't distinguish without more info:

Found it -- thanks for the extra detail, that pointed me at the right scenario (a wide table, scrolled right). Root cause is different from the shadow/border fix: table-scroll-wrap (the actual overflow:auto scroll container) had its own horizontal padding (padding: 0 28px) for the table's side margins. That's a well-known CSS scroll-container gotcha -- a scroll container's START-side padding gets 'consumed' the moment you scroll past 0; the visible scrollport clips exactly at the padding edge, so a non-frozen column sliding underneath can bleed into that 28px padding gap, uncovered by anything, since the sticky/frozen cells' own left:0 anchor doesn't extend backward to cover their container's own padding. That's the sliver you were seeing sticking out on the left as you scrolled right.

Fix: moved that 28px inset off table-scroll-wrap's padding and onto a margin on its non-scrolling parent (table-region) instead. A margin on a child is just normal scrollable content -- not a specially-clipped padding zone -- so there's no gap left for anything to bleed through. Verified live: scanned the actual painted element at multiple points in the table's left inset across 6 different scroll positions (0 through 1500px, with a wide 15-column table) -- zero non-frozen columns ever paint there anymore. Visual inset at rest is unchanged (still ~28px). Running the freeze-columns + interaction suites now before closing this out properly.

2. Fixed by moving that inset to a margin on the non-scrolling parent (table-region) instead -- a margin isn't subject to that scroll quirk. Verified by sampling the actual painted element at multiple points in the table's left inset across 6 scroll positions on a 15-column-wide table -- zero bleed-through now at any position.

Picking this back up -- two real issues here, both making sense now:

1. Border scope: my last fix drew a border on the LEFT edge of the gutter too (plus top-left/bottom-left corner rounding), to keep the table's own outer border/corner pinned to the frozen area as you scroll. That's created the 'full border around the frozen region' look you don't want. 2. The bigger one: my earlier fix for the 'sticking out on the left' bug moved the table's 28px side inset from padding (on the scroll container) to a MARGIN on table-region, which sits entirely OUTSIDE the scrollable area. A margin out there never scrolls, ever -- which is exactly the permanent 'gutter' you're now seeing regardless of freeze state, and why the table can no longer disappear fully off the window edges like it used to. The fix that actually gets both properties at once: move that 28px inset to a margin on the INNER scrolled content wrapper instead (still inside the scroll container, so it's genuinely part of the scrollable range and disappears off-screen normally when unfrozen) rather than on table-region (outside it). Root cause: frozen columns used position:sticky per cell. A sticky element can't stick past its own row's right edge -- so once scrolled far enough toward the true end of a wide table, the frozen columns silently detached and scrolled away with everything else. history.text:
Plan: this applies to every markdown-capable text surface in the app -- issue comments (new + edit), project comments (new + edit), project notes, and multiline text-type fields (shared editDraft state across the main grid cell / slideover description / slideover field-grid renderings of the same textarea).

- New pure helpers in wigwag-core.js: isPastedTextASingleUrl(text) (the ENTIRE trimmed clipboard content must be just a bare http(s) URL, nothing else -- pasting a paragraph that happens to contain a link shouldn't trigger this) and wrapSelectionWithMarkdownLink(value, selStart, selEnd, url) (pure string splice, returns the new full value with the selected slice replaced by '[selected](url)'). Both unit tested.
- New shared component method handleMarkdownLinkPaste(e, applyNewValue): reads the pasted text and the textarea/input's own native selectionStart/selectionEnd directly off the event target (works identically regardless of which specific field it's attached to) -- if there's no real selection, or the paste isn't a bare URL, does nothing and lets the browser's normal paste happen. Otherwise preventDefault and calls the caller-supplied applyNewValue(newText) closure, which is just the field's own existing one-line state setter.
- Wire sc-camel-on-paste at each of the 7 template locations (new-comment-input, comment-edit-input, project-comment-input, project-comment-edit-input, notes-textarea, and the 3 identical text-field-edit-textarea renderings sharing editDraft), each a one-line closure calling the shared handler with that field's own existing setter.

Live verification plan: select text in each surface type, paste a bare URL over it, confirm the result is '[selected](url)'; confirm pasting a URL with NOTHING selected still does a normal paste (no wrapping); confirm pasting non-URL text over a selection still does a normal replace (no wrapping). Durable tests added alongside the existing markdown-field test coverage.

Done. Pasting a bare URL over a real text selection now wraps that selection as [text](url) instead of replacing it -- covers every markdown-capable surface: issue comments (new + edit), project comments (new + edit), project notes, and multiline text-type fields (main grid, slideover description, slideover field grid all share the same editing path).

Matching rule: the clipboard content has to be JUST a bare http(s) URL -- nothing else. Pasting a whole sentence that happens to contain a link, or pasting with nothing selected, or pasting non-URL text over a selection, all fall through to a completely normal paste, untouched.

Implementation is two small pure helpers (isPastedTextASingleUrl, wrapSelectionWithMarkdownLink, both unit tested) plus one shared paste handler that reads the pasted text and the field's own selection range straight off the native event -- works identically on all 8 wiring points without needing to know which state key each field's draft lives under.

One real interaction surfaced in the full suite: an existing test used 'select all, then paste a URL' purely as a shortcut to REPLACE a field's whole value -- since that field already had real content, the new feature correctly wrapped it in a link instead of replacing it. Fixed the test (clear first, then paste at a collapsed cursor) rather than the feature, since wrapping a genuine selection is exactly what was asked for. New test file tests/paste-link-wraps-selection.spec.js (9 tests). Full suite (726 tests) passed clean.

history.value: Feature: surface keyword matches hidden by column filters

When the keyword filter (filterQuery) matches issues that the active column filters (columnFilters) are excluding, show a hint next to the filter box: "N match(es) hidden by column filters" + a "Clear column filters" link/button.

Behavior:

    Compute matches against keyword only (before column filters), then matches after column filters are applied. The difference count is what's hidden.
    Only show the hint when filterQuery is non-empty AND at least one column filter is active AND the hidden count > 0.
    "Clear column filters" resets columnFilters to {} (and persists it) — does not touch the keyword filter.
    Edge case: if the column filters exclude every keyword match (table would render completely empty), fall back to showing those hidden matches anyway, rendered at reduced opacity (~0.5), rather than leaving the table blank. No extra label/tag/icon on the faded rows — opacity alone is the signal. Append (shown faded below) to the hint text in this case.
    We considered a manual toggle to reveal hidden matches on demand (with a tag marking them), and rejected it — unnecessary complexity for a rare case. The faded fallback only kicks in automatically when the view would otherwise be empty.

Implementation reference (Issue Tracker.dc.html): in the issues-filtering pipeline, capture matchedByKeywordIssues/count right after the keyword filter and before the column-filter loop, diff against the post-column-filter result. If post-filter is empty and there were keyword matches, use matchedByKeywordIssues (tagged __dimmed: true) as the row set instead, and apply opacity: 0.5 per row when dimmed.

history.text:
Plan: implementing per the spec as written.

In the render pipeline, right after the keyword filter is applied and before column filters are applied, snapshot the keyword-matched issue set. Compute which of those get excluded by the (already-existing, frozen-snapshot) columnFilterExcludedIds -- that diff is exactly what's hidden. Show a pill next to the filter box (same visual family as the existing 'Frozen through X' / 'Grouped by X' pills) reading 'N match(es) hidden by column filters' with a 'Clear column filters' action that resets columnFilters to {} (persisted automatically via the existing componentDidUpdate persist cycle) and leaves the keyword filter untouched.

Edge case per spec: if column filters would leave the table completely empty despite real keyword matches, fall back to rendering those keyword matches anyway at 0.5 opacity (no icon/tag, opacity alone is the signal), and append '(shown faded below)' to the hint text. Scoping this whole feature to table view only, matching the spec's own framing ('the table would render completely empty') -- Kanban view shares the same underlying issue list but has no dimmed-card treatment and a different empty-state story, so it's left untouched (the hint pill itself won't show there either).

No manual reveal toggle, per the explicit 'considered and rejected' note in the description.

Will add durable Playwright coverage in tests/select-fields.spec.js or a new file (checking existing column-filter test locations first) for: the hint appears/count is correct, Clear column filters works, the dimmed fallback triggers only when the table would otherwise be empty, and it does NOT show in Kanban view. Full suite before marking this done.

Done. Implemented per spec:

- Right after the keyword filter is applied and before column filters apply, the pipeline now snapshots the keyword-matched issue set and diffs it against the (existing, frozen-snapshot) columnFilterExcludedIds to get exactly what's hidden.
- A pill next to the filter box (same visual family as the existing 'Frozen through X'/'Grouped by X' pills) reads 'N match(es) hidden by column filters', shown only when filterQuery is non-empty, at least one column filter is active, and the hidden count is > 0.
- 'Clear column filters' resets columnFilters to {} (persisted automatically through the existing save cycle) and leaves the keyword filter untouched.
- Edge case: if the column filters would leave the table completely empty despite real keyword matches, falls back to showing those matches anyway at 0.5 opacity (no icon/tag -- opacity alone is the signal, per the spec), with '(shown faded below)' appended to the hint text.
- No manual reveal toggle, per the 'considered and rejected' note.
- Scoped to table view only -- Kanban shares the same underlying issue list but has no dimmed-card treatment and wasn't part of the ask, so the hint/fallback don't apply there.

6 new tests in tests/interaction.spec.js ('Hidden keyword matches (column filters)', right after the existing 'Column value filters' block): no-hint cases (keyword only, column filter only, filter doesn't actually hide anything), the normal hint+restore case, the dimmed-fallback case, and confirming neither the hint nor the fallback leak into Kanban view. Full suite (742 tests) passed clean.

The header looks like ass in dark mode

Header dark mode fixes

Problem: The header's colorful triangle-mesh background used a fixed white 55%-opacity wash (added for light-mode text legibility over the mesh). In dark mode this stayed pure white against the dark UI, clashing badly with the rest of the theme. On top of that, several breadcrumb elements (identity label, "/" separator, project name, chevron) used hardcoded dark greys (#45454d, #2c2c33, var(--n30)), which had fine contrast against the old white wash but became nearly invisible once any dark tint sat behind them — contrast measured ~1.4:1, far under the 4.5:1 minimum.

Fix:

    Introduced a theme-aware --header-mesh-wash token: white/55% opacity in light mode, a dark near-black/60% opacity wash in dark mode — so the mesh pattern recedes into the dark surface instead of glowing white.
    Replaced the breadcrumb's hardcoded colors with var(--ink-on-accent) — the existing design-system token for text on colored/accent surfaces — applied to the identity label, "/", project name, and chevron, with the separator/chevron slightly dimmed via opacity for visual hierarchy.

Result: In dark mode, the header mesh now tints dark instead of white, and all breadcrumb text reads bright, near-white, and legible against it — matching how the app already renders text on other accent-colored surfaces.

history.text: Plan: adding a theme-aware --header-mesh-wash CSS variable (white/55% in light mode, near-black/60% in dark mode) to replace the hardcoded white wash over the header mesh, and swapping the breadcrumb's hardcoded dark-grey colors (identity label, /, project name, chevron) for var(--ink-on-accent), dimming the separator and chevron slightly via opacity for hierarchy. Rolling this in alongside other header/scrollbar work already in flight this session; will run the full test suite before marking done.

Done: added a theme-aware --header-mesh-wash token (white/55% light, near-black/60% dark) and swapped the breadcrumb's hardcoded dark greys for var(--text-primary) instead of the originally-suggested var(--ink-on-accent) -- live-verified via screenshot that ink-on-accent is white in BOTH themes (it's meant for text on opaque accent fills like buttons, not this light/dark-washed mesh), which made light mode nearly illegible. text-primary genuinely flips per theme (dark-on-light / near-white-on-dark) and still lands on the dark-mode result the fix wanted. Rewrote the two header-mesh.spec.js tests that covered the old fixed-ink behavior to assert the new theme-following behavior instead (also fixed a latent bug in their own luminance helper: this app's oklch()-authored colors come back from getComputedStyle as oklch(...) strings, not rgb(...), so the old regex-based rgb-luminance math was silently computing garbage that happened to pass by coincidence). Full test suite run pending.

history.value: I'd like a new column type - called something like a comment thread. In the table view it just renders the latest update, with a neat timestamp.

history.text:
Design conclusions from discussion with Tom (2026-09-15):

CONCEPT: a generic "comment stream" field type, not a one-off "update" column. An issue can have any number of comment-stream fields (e.g. "Update", "My actions", "Comments"), each an independent append-only, timestamped, signed entry log -- same underlying mechanism regardless of name. Table cell shows the latest entry + a relative timestamp; full history is retained and viewable (slide-over, same shape as today's comment thread).

MOTIVATING USE CASE: Tom wants an "Update" column showing the next thing to share with the customer (latest entry visible at a glance in the grid), with history retained -- without diluting the existing Comments field's role as a scrappy running-notes capture. "My actions" is a second instance of the same need.

DECISION: fold the existing special-cased Comments thread into this new generic type, rather than maintaining both mechanisms side by side long-term. Comments becomes field id 'comments' of the new comment-stream type, given special UI placement (comment-indicator gutter column, prominent slide-over slot) by convention -- exactly the same pattern `description` already uses (an ordinary field, specially placed). This means no data migration: today's `issue.comments` array becomes the value backing that same well-known field id, synthesized on load for old files the same way description/title presumably already are.

RESOLVED:
- Mentions/notifications are uniform across every comment-stream field -- an @mention in "My actions" notifies exactly like one in "Comments". No per-field opt-in/out.
- "My actions" (and any other named instance) is a normal shared/collaborative field, edited by whoever's driving the issue -- not private-to-one-viewer. Wigwag has no per-user private state today, and this doesn't introduce any.

OPEN / NOT YET DECIDED (worth settling before implementation):
- Naming: "comment stream" was Tom's working name, not confirmed final.
- Exact per-entry data shape -- presumably identical to today's comment entries (signed, timestamped, author identity, text), just keyed under a field id instead of the issue-level array.
- Export behavior (CSV/XLSX/plain JSONL "View source"): latest entry only, full thread flattened, or excluded entirely? Not discussed yet.
- Whether a comment-stream field can be bound/derived the way other field types can (almost certainly no -- these are inherently manually-authored streams, not values a rule computes -- but worth stating explicitly in the eventual spec).

OUT OF SCOPE (filed separately): "local-only fields" that never leave the current instance/never sync -- a different, format-level mechanism Tom raised in passing. Filed as #109 (cf6075aa), explicitly deferred, not bundled into this work.

Implementation plan (2026-09-15):

STORAGE: a new per-issue `commentStreams: { [fieldId]: [entries...] }` map, replacing today's top-level `comments` array entirely (same entry shape: id/author/email/time/text/sortKey/sig/sigRedacted/pubKey). Migration is automatic and one-time-effectively: `hydrateIssue` (runs on both localStorage load and file import/merge) moves `issue.comments` into `commentStreams.comments` and drops the old key. No dual-support path kept around afterward.

FIELD TYPE: new `commentStream` type (label "Comment stream" in Add Field). Not bindable, no options -- same restriction date fields already have.

COMMENTS ITSELF: gets a real `fieldDefs.comments` entry (type commentStream), synthesized on load for any project that doesn't already have one (an unsigned, legacy-backfill-style projectHistory entry documents the synthesis, same pattern as existing migration backfills). Scope decision, flagging a deliberate deviation from "exactly like description": the comment-indicator gutter column keeps its current fixed position via the existing `__comments__` sentinel mechanism (freeze columns, drag-reorder etc. are unaffected) -- only its DATA SOURCE and label lookup change, not its position. Making it a fully ordinary, reorderable column would mean reworking the sentinel/freeze/drag infrastructure for no functional gain you asked for, so I'm leaving that alone.

NEW FIELDS (e.g. "Update", "My actions"): ordinary columns. Cell shows latest entry's text (truncated) + a relative timestamp, or a muted "No updates yet". Clicking opens the slide-over, which gets a section per such field: entry list (newest first, markdown-rendered, edit-your-own-entry) plus an add-entry composer -- same interaction shape comments already have, just generalized and repeated per field.

MENTIONS/MERGE/EXPORT: mention-notification scanning covers every commentStream field uniformly (per our earlier agreement). Merge unions each field's entries independently by id, same algorithm as today's comment union, just keyed per field now. JSONL export carries `commentStreams` instead of `comments`. CSV/XLSX export a commentStream field as its latest entry's plain text, matching how other complex field types flatten to a display string. Bulk actions and column-value-filtering exclude commentStream fields (doesn't make sense to bulk-overwrite or filter-by-current-value on an append-only thread).

Will update docs/FORMAT.md and add a new tests/comment-stream-fields.spec.js, then run the full suite before calling this done.

Done. Full suite: 755 passed, 0 failed.

Summary of what shipped:
- New commentStream field type (label "Comment stream" in Add Field). Not bindable, no options.
- Storage: issue.commentStreams[fieldId], an array per field, same signed entry shape comments always used. Automatic one-time migration from the old top-level `comments` array on load (hydrateIssue), with no dual-support kept afterward.
- "Comments" folded into the same mechanism: every project gets a commentStream field synthesized as id 'comments' if it doesn't already have one, backed by the existing __comments__ sentinel for its fixed gutter position (position stays special; storage/mechanism doesn't).
- Table cell: latest entry, markdown-rendered, plus a relative timestamp. Offers "Wrap text" like any text-like column (line-clamp via the same mechanism plain text fields use). Empty state shows "No updates yet".
- Slide-over: full entry history per field, newest first, markdown-rendered, with the same edit-your-own-entry/redact affordances comments always had, plus an add-entry composer.
- Mentions and per-issue-subscription notifications are uniform across every comment-stream field.
- Merge unions each field's entries independently. JSONL export carries commentStreams. CSV/XLSX export the latest entry's text. Bulk "set field" excludes comment-stream fields.
- docs/FORMAT.md updated; new tests/comment-stream-fields.spec.js (13 tests) plus fixes to 8 pre-existing tests across 4 files that read the old shape directly.

Two real bugs found and fixed during regression testing (both now covered by tests):
- addIssue wasn't initializing commentStreams on new issues, crashing every "add a new row" flow.
- Clicking edit/redact inside the slide-over's comment-stream section bubbled up to the same onCellClick that opens the slide-over, silently resetting the in-progress edit. openSlideOver is now a no-op when the same issue is already open and visible.

Nothing committed yet -- let me know if you'd like this committed.

UX rework (2026-09-15), from the comment_stream.zip design handoff:

TABLE CELL: click now uses the same two-click select-then-commit gate as
every other popover-backed cell type, and opens a small posting popover
right there (280px, viewport-clamped using its own real width, "Post an
update…" placeholder, ⌘/Ctrl+Enter submits, closes on post/outside-click/
Escape) -- no need to open the slide-over just to add an update.

SLIDE-OVER FIELD BLOCK: now display-only -- latest entry (still markdown-
rendered) plus a "View updates" link that jumps the Activity area to a
dedicated tab for that field. No inline composer here any more (that was
the "unpolished" v1 behaviour from the original build).

ACTIVITY TABS: a generic tab -- one per commentStream-typed field on the
issue -- is now inserted between the fixed "Comments" and "History" tabs,
labeled from the field's own name with a live count (e.g. "UPDATE (3)").
That tab is where the full entry history, the add-entry composer, and
edit-your-own-entry/redact all live now, reusing the exact same
entry/edit/redact markup and testids the Comments tab always used
(comment-edit-btn/activity-redact-btn/comment-edit-input/etc.), just
parameterized by field id instead of hardcoded to 'comments'. Only one
composer is ever shown at a time -- Comments tab shows its box, a stream
tab shows its own (separate draft state), History shows neither.

Storage/data model is unchanged from the original build (commentStreams
map, same signed-entry shape) -- this was purely a UI/interaction pass.

Two real, pre-existing bugs found via live verification and fixed:
1. The outside-click-closes-popover allowlist only ever recognized
   select/multiselect field types, so the comment-stream popover never
   closed on an outside click (present since the original build, only
   now noticed because the popover is the primary posting surface).
2. The Comments/History tab-bar's inactive-tab spans were each gated on
   the OTHER tab's flag (a safe shortcut back when exactly one of the two
   was always true) -- so activating a third (stream) tab made BOTH the
   Comments and History labels vanish from the DOM entirely. Fixed by
   gating each on the negation of its own flag instead.

Verified live via ad-hoc Playwright scripts (popover open/post/dismiss,
outside-click, field-block preview + jump link, tab bar order/counts,
posting/editing/redacting from the new tab, single-composer gating) and
rewrote tests/comment-stream-fields.spec.js for the new interaction model
(16 tests). Full suite: 758 passed, 1 confirmed pre-existing flake
(tests/deep-links.spec.js's Escape/history.back test -- fails only under
full-suite load, passes reliably in isolation both with and without
today's changes, and passes on HEAD with none of today's changes applied
either) plus the two documented (KNOWN GAP) staleness tests, unrelated to
this work. docs/FORMAT.md's "Comment stream fields" section updated to
describe the new interaction model.
